item.title: Setting limits on phase transitions in the dark energy era
item.description: The universe is known to be expanding at an accelerating rate. Physicists typically attribute this acceleration to dark energy, a mysterious component of the universe that exerts negative pressure, causing space to expand faster. Dark energy is thought to have become the predominant influence on the universe's evolution around 3–4 billion years ago, at the beginning of what is known as the dark energy era. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study finds sustainable farming program helps refugees, immigrants boost health while launching agribusinesses
item.description: The slang term "touch grass" encourages people to step away from the internet or devices and connect with the real world. New research from the University of Kansas has found that a project that helps resettled refugees and immigrants learn sustainable farming has many of the term's same benefits, improving people's mental and physical well-being and training them to run independent agricultural businesses. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The hidden chemistry behind glow-in-the-dark art
item.description: Some of the world's brightest colors don't just reflect light; they create it. Scientists and museum conservators are now uncovering why these luminous pigments fade and how to preserve them for future generations. The findings could help protect artwork while informing the development of longer-lasting phosphorescent materials for a variety of applications, from fashion runways to airport runways. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Namibia paves way for phosphate mining in the Atlantic Ocean
item.description: Namibia has granted environmental clearance for an offshore phosphate mining project that paves the way for the world's first commercial seabed-dredging operation for the mineral, despite opposition from green groups and the fishing industry. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tides can vary by almost a meter across a single bay, four decades of satellite images reveal
item.description: Tide levels can vary by almost a meter across a single bay, according to a new study that uses decades of satellite images to measure tides at the scale of individual beaches. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bright ideas accelerate the hunt for quantum emitters
item.description: The search for materials that can power future quantum technologies is accelerating, but identifying the most promising candidates remains painfully slow. Evaluating whether a material can efficiently emit quantum light requires computationally intensive simulations, making it difficult to screen the vast number of available materials. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tens of thousands flee fire near U.S. city of Reno
item.description: Tens of thousands of people looked set to spend another night away from home Monday as a wind-driven fire bore down on the western U.S. city of Reno. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Después de años escuchando lo contrario, este estudio finlandés dice que pasar mucho tiempo frente a una pantalla favorece el rendimiento cognitivo
item.description: En 2007, en la ciudad finlandesa de Kuopio, un equipo de investigadores reclutaron a poco más de 500 niños de entre 7 y 9 años. Su idea era responder a una pregunta aparentemente sencilla : ¿cuánto influye moverse en el desarrollo de los niños? Durante el estudio, midieron la actividad física, midieron la dieta y, casi de propina, preguntaron por las horas que pasaban haciendo determinadas cosas. Entre ellas, mirando pantallas. Ocho años después, cuando trataron de ver cómo iba el desarrollo cognitivo de los 260 participantes que estaban aún vinculados al proyecto, los investigadores se… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: In 2014, scientists set off 23 blasts to uncover magma hidden beneath Mount St Helens
item.description: In a groundbreaking study, researchers utilized controlled explosions paired with seismic technology to investigate Mount St. Helens' subterranean magma systems. They discovered a magma-reservoir located between four to fifteen kilometers deep. This extensive analysis employed numerous instruments to track seismic waves within the volcano, yielding vital knowledge about magma movements. Such understanding is instrumental in forecasting volcanic activity and potential eruptions. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Meet Jeremiah Bents, the Minnesota student who recreated Mars soil to test water cleanup
item.description: Jeremiah Bents, a Minnesota student, explored water filtration using Mars soil simulant. His project examined ammonia removal from contaminated water in a laboratory setting. This innovative work earned him the Earth Systems Science Award at a state science fair. He received guidance from university researchers and a NASA scientist. Bents' experiment demonstrated a practical application for future space missions. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Scientists turn plastic waste into protein cookies; food can tackle hunger and feed space crews
item.description: Researchers at Southern Illinois University Carbondale are developing protein-rich cookies made using plastic waste and agricultural waste. Called µBites, the cookies use PET plastic from bottles and discarded corn stalks and leaves. Programmed yeasts convert processed waste into proteins, fats, acids and flavouring molecules. The NASA-linked project is aimed at developing food for resource-limited environments, including future deep-space missions. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

These hidden lakes were found to fill and drain over short periods. This dynamic water system influences ice stream speeds and mass balance. The findings showed a hidden, active world beneath the frozen continent. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Process doubles the size of PFAS molecules, making them easy to destroy
item.description: Ask a chemist to name the strongest single bond in organic chemistry, and they'll likely say carbon-fluorine. It's that bond, repeated dozens of times over, that gives per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) their nickname: forever chemicals. Manufacturers prize PFAS for the same reason regulators dread them. The bonds barely break down, which is exactly why the compounds are so good at repelling water, oil and heat in everything from semiconductor fabrication to nonstick cookware. This is also why PFAS persist in soil, water and living tissue long after serving their industrial purpose. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What would happen to human interaction if AI could read our emotions?
item.description: AI systems are increasingly being developed to recognize emotions by analyzing facial expressions, voices, body language and other physiological signals. Although the scientific validity of many of these systems remains contested, they are already being tested in health care and security settings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Blood-clotting protein may be SARS-CoV-2's hidden accomplice, helping it hide from antibodies and reach blood vessels
item.description: Fibrinogen, the abundant plasma protein best known for forming blood clots, may play a second and far less benign role during SARS-CoV-2 infection: acting as a molecular bridge that simultaneously hides the virus from neutralizing antibodies and delivers it to the cells lining blood vessels. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Natural gas drilling could raise salt levels, in turn boosting radium in water
item.description: Pennsylvania ranks second in U.S. natural gas production, accounting for about one-fifth of U.S. output in 2024, and has one of the most extensive histories of energy extraction in the country. A team of researchers from Penn State is trying to better understand the environmental impacts of these sites—specifically, whether fracking is increasing radium content in local drinking water. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA starshade would enable astronomers to directly image rocky exoworlds
item.description: A NASA-led team hopes to take a shortcut to direct imaging of extrasolar Earth-like planets. The idea is to use what they call a hybrid telescope composed of an orbital starshade coupled with the next-generation extremely large ground-based optical telescopes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Meteorite dust holds records of magnetism that may have helped form the sun
item.description: Around 4.6 billion years ago, the solar system was little more than a giant ball of gas and dust. Over the next few million years, this "solar nebula" underwent a huge transformation, flattening into a disk of matter that then condensed to form the central sun and orbiting planets. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How fusion reactions can survive flaws—up to a point
item.description: Researchers at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have found that implosions designed for inertial fusion energy (IFE) can tolerate significant imperfections before performance abruptly declines, a finding that could inform the design of fuel targets for future fusion power plants. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.description: Researchers at TU Dortmund University, Paderborn University, the University of Duisburg-Essen, and the University of Oxford have developed a new method for selectively modifying the internal structure of specific types of glass. The study, published in the journal Nature Materials, shows how adding an organic molecule during melting causes the chemical bonds in the material to rearrange. The process reduces the required processing temperature, prevents the substance from decomposing, and allows the magnetic and optical properties to be precisely tuned. item.title: Wildlife trafficking spreads across social media, putting thousands of species at risk
item.description: Researchers monitoring online activity for six weeks in mid-2025 found primates, birds, snakes, frogs, orchids and many other wildlife groups advertised for sale across Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube. Wildlife is increasingly being trafficked through online platforms. Online illegal wildlife trade poses significant risks to species, ecosystems, and animal and public health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Human rights rankings reveal surprising over- and underperformers
item.description: When it comes to human rights, it probably won't surprise you that Scandinavian countries perform well by statistical measures, along with Canada and Australia. But did you know that Mozambique, the Philippines, and Rwanda are also considered "overperformers," meaning that they score higher on human rights than expected? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Temperature-tunable micropillars enable programmable sorting of particles and cells
item.description: A programmable microfluidic device developed at the Institute of Science Tokyo, Japan, combines deterministic lateral displacement, a microfluidic technique used to separate particles according to size, with temperature-responsive polymer micropillars to dynamically change separation conditions along a single channel. Using this device, researchers successfully separated multiple particle populations. Additionally, they efficiently isolated viable cancer cells, white blood cells and red blood cells from diluted whole blood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A bird's eye view of illegal logging and its consequences in the Peruvian Amazon
item.description: When I first arrived in Peru's Allpahuayo-Mishana National Reserve in 2005, a local youth surprised me with an offer to sell me a live owl, despite the fact that we were in a protected area where commercial hunting was prohibited. We set the owl free together, but this turned out to be an early lesson about the vulnerability of tropical protected areas to exploitation, even when laws and policies had been put in place to protect them. At that time, Allpahuayo-Mishana was a newly designated protected area with no paid staff except for its director, who was stationed in the nearby city of… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI finds six ways to print rocket-grade alloy on commercial 3D printers
item.description: Washington State University researchers used artificial intelligence to find a more efficient, less expensive way to 3D-print a high-performance metal alloy, saving researchers from needing to painstakingly test more than 100 million options. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deuterium enables chip waveguides to generate broadband light from infrared pulses
item.description: A research team from Singapore, led by Associate Professor Dawn Tan of the Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD) and Dr. Luo Xianshu, head of the Silicon Photonics Department at the A*STAR Institute of Microelectronics (A*STAR IME), has developed a low-loss silicon nitride waveguide that generates broadband light on a chip. By replacing hydrogen with its heavier isotope, deuterium, the team fabricated the low-loss SiN waveguide on an 8-inch wafer using a low-temperature process, demonstrating its potential for large-scale manufacturing and integration with CMOS-compatible… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bacteria from ancestral wheat microbiomes help protect plants against root rot fungus
item.description: In the journal npj Biofilms and Microbiomes, researchers from the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (EMBRAPA) and the University of São Paulo (USP) describe the role of three bacteria in suppressing a soil-borne wheat pathogen that causes root rot. The study paves the way for the development of inoculants that can be used in agriculture. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Metal ceramics under AI control: A new approach for calculating the mechanical properties of materials
item.description: Researchers from the Skoltech Materials Center have proposed a new approach to modeling the mechanical properties of heterogeneous materials, combining machine learning with active learning on local chemical configurations. The method enables calculations of large systems containing tens of thousands of atoms with accuracy comparable to direct quantum-mechanical calculations (DFT), but without requiring extensive computational resources. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How atmospheric dryness limits increases in typhoon rainfall
item.description: Under global warming, scientists have widely expected tropical cyclones (including typhoons and hurricanes) to bring more intense and frequent rainfall. The underlying physics seems intuitive: Rising temperatures allow the atmosphere to hold more moisture, which, combined with intensifying storms, should theoretically trigger more destructive downpours. However, when researchers analyze climate model projections, they encounter a puzzling phenomenon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Woodlands and other natural spaces could help cities cope with extreme heat
item.description: Green and blue spaces, such as woodlands and riversides, could provide a vital line of defense for cities facing increasingly hot summers, according to new research from the University of Surrey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New study reveals how space rocks become meteorites
item.description: What happens to a space rock as it falls through Earth's atmosphere and becomes a meteorite? By studying 75 meteorite falls captured on video and in photographs, researchers identified seven distinct phases in the journey from space rock to meteorite. Their findings show that melting and fragmentation, rather than simply evaporation and "burning up," control how a rock loses mass, slows down and ultimately reaches the ground. The journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science published these findings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers dodge crocs to probe coral bleaching after technology failed
item.description: Researchers confirm a 2024 coral bleaching event in remote, crocodile-inhabited Northern Territory waters was not picked up by the latest predictive technologies. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: La pasta del futuro: cómo el trigo italiano enfrenta el cambio climático
item.description: La pasta es uno de los alimentos más apreciados del mundo, pero el cambio climático amenaza uno de sus ingredientes esenciales: el trigo. En Emilia-Romaña, conocida como la "Food Valley" de Italia, investigadores trabajan en variedades de trigo capaces de resistir el aumento de las temperaturas y condiciones climáticas cada vez más extremas. El objetivo: desarrollar la pasta del futuro y preservar uno de los grandes símbolos de la gastronomía italiana. Nuestro equipo periodístico nos cuenta desde el terreno cómo la ciencia busca hacer posible esta transformación. Fuente: France 24 - Español.

item.title: Vacuum-fluctuation-enhanced superconductivity demonstrated for the first time
item.description: In a study published in Nature on Aug. 19, a research team has enhanced superconductivity through vacuum fluctuations for the first time. The achievement marks a significant advance in controlling quantum states of matter. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Sets Coverage for Roman Space Telescope Launch from Florida
item.description: Coverage plans are ready for NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope prelaunch and launch activities. Roman is NASA’s next-generation observatory designed to explore some of the universe’s biggest mysteries, including dark energy. NASA and SpaceX are targeting Roman’s liftoff for no earlier than 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday, Aug. 30, aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Jessica Taveau

item.title: Chemicals banned in the 1970s still widely detected across Europe, new study finds
item.description: A new study has found that regulatory restrictions introduced more than half a century ago have failed to eliminate contamination from banned chemicals across Europe. Researchers say they detected banned chemicals in air, water, sediments, soils, snow and sludge, demonstrating their environmental persistence. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Assembly of giant wild sunflower family genomes unlocks potential for new perennial crops
item.description: The Land Institute and HudsonAlpha Institute for Biotechnology, in collaboration with key partners, have assembled the first chromosome-scale, haplotype-phased genomes for Silphium integrifolium (rosinweed, silflower) and Silphium perfoliatum (cup plant, silphie). This landmark research promises to expand and accelerate the development of more climate-resilient, sustainable perennial crops. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Shell-crushing predators may have sparked early Cenozoic boom in marine snail evolution
item.description: A large-scale study of nearly 700 species reveals the evolutionary relationships and history of Neogastropoda, a diverse group of marine snails. The findings provide new evidence for their single origin, identify four new families and reveal a previously undetected burst of diversification in the early Cenozoic. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When to trust the experts? Follow these guidelines to evaluate science on any topic
item.description: When should we trust the evidence and the experts who interpret it for us? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Glacier retreat could promote the spread of diseases among bees
item.description: A study conducted in the Swiss Alps by the University of Lausanne and the University of Milan shows that glacier retreat and changing vegetation could influence the spread of certain pathogens between honeybees and wild bees. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Marker words suggest sharp rise in AI-assisted biomedical writing after ChatGPT
item.description: Up until two years ago, using large language models was still considered a special skill that everyone was encouraged to learn. Now, it is ubiquitous, especially in writing research papers that eventually become part of the scientific knowledge we build around a subject. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Women and racialized CEOs may outperform their peers because they face tougher barriers to the top
item.description: Every so often, a headline declares that women make better leaders. A widely cited 2019 Harvard Business Review analysis, for instance, found women outscored men on most leadership competencies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The 'wonder material' graphene can be made using a kitchen blender, a mobile phone and a newspaper
item.description: There is something slightly ridiculous about using a kitchen blender to make graphene. This is, after all, the "wonder material" associated with futuristic technologies. You might reasonably expect its production to involve equally futuristic equipment. Often, it does. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gut bacteria mostly compete—but cooperation finds a way
item.description: Understanding how bacteria influence one another is essential for understanding how microbial communities are formed and maintained. Researchers at Umeå University have now systematically mapped interactions between common gut bacteria, creating one of the most comprehensive datasets of its kind. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What Gen Z‑led uprisings across Asia reveal about the strengths and limitations of youth protest
item.description: Recent Gen Z-led uprisings have reshaped political narratives across Asia, raising a pointed question: Can street-level youth outrage be transformed into governing power and lasting institutional change? Or does it burn out once the protests end? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Dung beetles offer insights into biodiversity in Singapore
item.description: Dung beetles could provide scientists with a new way to uncover the animals living in Singapore's forests, including elusive species that are difficult to spot with conventional wildlife surveys. NTU researchers found that DNA preserved in the insects' guts can reveal the mammals, birds and other vertebrates whose waste they have fed on. Fuente: Phys.org.
